overview.headline: Water moves through evaporation, condensation and runoff

keyPoints.point: Students learn that the water cycle moves water from ground to atmosphere and back.
keyPoints.quote: At its core, the water cycle is the motion of the water from the ground to the atmosphere and back again.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that evaporation is the change of liquid substance into gas state.
keyPoints.quote: Evaporation is the change of state in a substance from a liquid to a gas.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that transpiration is evaporation of water from plants through stomata.
keyPoints.quote: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from plants through stomata.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that condensation changes water vapor into liquid state.
keyPoints.quote: Condensation is the process whereby water vapor is changed into a liquid state.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that precipitation can be rain, hail, snow or sleet.
keyPoints.quote: Precipitation can be in the form of rain, hail, snow, or sleet.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that rivers and lakes are results of runoff.
keyPoints.quote: Rivers and lakes are results of runoff.

keyTerms.gloss: Change from liquid to gas that needs energy to occur
keyTerms.quote: Evaporation is the change of state in a substance from a liquid to a gas.

keyTerms.gloss: Evaporation of water from plants through leaf openings
keyTerms.quote: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from plants through stomata.

keyTerms.gloss: Process where water vapor changes into liquid state
keyTerms.quote: Condensation is the process whereby water vapor is changed into a liquid state.

keyTerms.gloss: Fresh water that falls as rain, hail, snow or sleet
keyTerms.quote: Precipitation can be in the form of rain, hail, snow, or sleet.

keyTerms.gloss: Water that flows when ground is saturated and cannot absorb more
keyTerms.quote: Runoff occurs when there is excessive precipitation and the ground is saturated (cannot absorb any more water).
